metadata.title: A Speed-Accuracy Response Model with Conditional Dependence Between Items
metadata.venue: Quantitative Psychology (Springer Proceedings in Mathematics & Statistics)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This chapter does not use an ILSA/PISA/TIMSS/PIRLS-style complex survey design with sampling weights; instead, it applies cognitive measurement modeling to a test dataset (listening test) with item-level response data. The estimation is based on conditional maximum likelihood / pairwise conditional maximum likelihood procedures (CML/PCML) and does not describe any application of sampling weights or replicate-weight variance estimation. Because no survey design variables (e.g., school/strata/cluster weights) are reported, analysts should treat the dataset as an unweighted measurement sample unless the original test documentation specifies otherwise. The chapter also does not report any plausible-values generation or PV pooling, so weighting guidance is limited to the measurement-model estimation context.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variables are item response scores derived from a speed-accuracy scoring rule (continuous SRT-based scores) and the model is an item-response measurement model, not an ILSA achievement scale with PVs. Missing-data handling is not reported because the chapter focuses on model formulation and estimation (CML/PCML) and does not describe any explicit missingness mechanism, imputation, or deletion rule for incomplete item responses in the applied listening-test example. This is a reporting gap for transparency about how incomplete response patterns were treated in the empirical illustration.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used an empirical listening-test dataset for non-native speakers with 17 items; the chapter reports the sample size n = 9355 and constructs item time limits d_j from the 99th percentile of empirical response-time distributions. No additional inclusion/exclusion criteria (e.g., grade bands, language background filters, or response-completeness rules) are described in the provided text.

data.outcome_summary: This chapter develops and illustrates a speed-accuracy response model that relaxes local independence by allowing conditional dependence between items, extending the Maris–van der Maas framework. The empirical illustration uses 17 listening-test items for non-native speakers and applies pairwise conditional maximum likelihood (PCML) to estimate item parameters under the proposed conditional-dependence model, with comparisons to Rasch and Haberman interaction models and to marginal maximum likelihood (MML) for the Maris–van der Maas model. The reported results are primarily parameter-estimation agreement checks: PCML yields item-parameter estimates very similar to CML (Rasch/Haberman) and to MML (Maris–van der Maas), and the estimated beta parameters are very similar across the Maris–van der Maas and proposed model. The chapter does not report predictive ML metrics (e.g., accuracy/RMSE) or survey-weighted inference, and it does not use ILSA-style plausible values.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is a measurement-model methodology chapter rather than an ILSA predictive ML study: it does not train predictive algorithms on ILSA achievement PVs, and it does not report ML performance metrics tied to a student-level prediction target. Consequently, fields such as ML techniques, confounders, and main findings in the ILSA ML schema are intentionally left empty because the chapter’s contribution is theoretical/estimation-method development and parameter recovery checks rather than predictive modeling outcomes.
